title: Interbranch Representation
text:
Abstract

This book advances and measures the concept of interbranch representation—how Members of Congress work directly with federal agencies on behalf of various constituencies. Interbranch representation includes casework (constituency service) on behalf of individuals, nonprofits, and businesses, as well as oversight and engaging in executive-branch policymaking and implementation. While many members of the public—and certainly the punditry—are aware of Congress’s legislative woes, fewer are aware of the other half of the work that congressional offices do behind the scenes to help constituents and shape executive-branch policymaking. We find that, collectively, members of Congress make over a hundred thousand requests a year directly to executive branch officials. At a time when policymaking as well as implementation is concentrated in the executive branch, the ombudsman role of congressional offices is a key facet of representation, and most congressional offices invest as much or more in interbranch work as they do in legislative work.
There are, however, massive differences in how much interbranch representation congressional offices provide. To explain this variation, we offer a framework with three types of explanations, those rooted in constituent demand, congressional office capacity, and strategic incentives. Rather than constituent demand and capacity constraints presenting trade-offs among representing different constituencies, we find higher-capacity congressional offices doing more of all types of interbranch representation. Differing levels of constituent demand matter, but most of the variation is due to different legislator capacity, particularly experience in office and committee positions that grant legislators access to additional information and staff. The main form of strategic behavior we find—legislators working much more with agencies perceived as being ideologically aligned—is consistent with a view of agencies and legislators as policy-making-and-implementing coalitions.  This does not explain representation of business interests, which has different drivers than other types of interbranch representation. One of those drivers is partisanship, with moderate Republicans doing substantially more for business, while more right-wing legislators provide less interbranch representation of all kinds, including less work on behalf of business. We find mixed evidence for other types of strategic behavior, such as reelection-motivated constituency service and interbranch work as a substitute for legislating when one’s party is out of power.
In sum, partisanship and ideology affect choices about which agencies legislators contact and on whose behalf. But variation in interbranch representation is mostly a story of the capacity of legislators, their offices, and committees, with varying levels of constituent demand often a secondary cause. We argue that a focus on interbranch representation adds important nuance to modern narratives about a broken Congress. While Congress may be broken in many ways, one underappreciated way in which Congress still works is through interbranch representation (at least for some districts). But American citizens, just like political scientists and journalists, haven’t been paying attention to the large amount of work Congress has been doing to advocate on their behalf.

title: 1  Interbranch Representation
text:
1.1 What is Interbranch Representation?
In the first few weeks of 2024, the Office of Legislation within the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) received 25 letters from members of Congress. These letters are part of a routine, quiet, but crucial undercurrent of legislative-executive interactions that exists beneath higher-profile hearings and investigations—forms of interactions between Congress and the bureaucracy with which the public is decidedly more familiar. A handful of these letters to the FDA in early 2024 concerned policy, as hearings and investigations usually do. For example, Representative Dan Goldman wrote with concerns about a rule that the FDA had recently proposed to regulate Laboratory Developed Tests (LDTs), and Senator Dick Durbin wrote regarding the FDA’s enforcement of the Tobacco Control Act. Most of the other letters, however, were written on behalf of individual constituents. Members of Congress shared correspondence from constituents who were asking for help obtaining necessary medication, asking for more information about drug shortages, drug trials, compassionate use, and obscure treatments for their medical conditions, and, in one case, urging that a canine dental stick product be removed from the market after it led to the death of their dog.
The personal stories contained in these letters conjure pictures of constituents turning to congressional offices for help with some of the most significant struggles of their lives. Moreover, they speak to the important role that communications with the bureaucracy can play in congressional representation. These 25 letters are a minuscule fraction of the hundreds of thousands that members of Congress collectively send to federal agencies every year. Veterans seek assistance from their legislators with obtaining healthcare and benefits from the Department of Veterans’ Affairs (VA), and families seek records of their loved ones’ military service from the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA). Numerous subagencies within the Department of Labor (DOL) handle requests to assist constituents with obtaining workers’ compensation payments, back pay, and coverage for medications and medical procedures. Each year, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) within the Department of Homeland Security receives hundreds of thousands of requests to assist legislators’ constituents with immigration matters, including student visas, foreign worker authorizations, and requests for asylum. All of these examples show members of Congress engaging in a deeply meaningful form of responsiveness that the public at large rarely has the opportunity to see.
The responsiveness evident through these communications stands in stark contrast to the version of Congress that exists in the minds of a public that disapproves of the institution at a rate of nearly 85%. A majority of survey respondents describe “most members of Congress” as corrupt, out of touch, and catering to special interests.1 Very little of Congress’s behind-the-scenes correspondence with the bureaucracy, however, supports these assumptions. Beyond writing to federal agencies on behalf of individual constituents, legislators write on behalf of small businesses who are seeking help navigating bureaucratic processes like grant applications and worker visas. Legislators also frequently write in support of nonprofit organizations and local governments seeking grants to help improve their communities. Correspondence about policy, even on behalf of entire industries, often concerns routine matters like rulemaking or testimony at hearings. Contrary to what we might assume about communications that take place out of view of the public, this “hidden half of Congress” contains little work that most constituents would find objectionable.
Potentially concerning, however, is the fact that some members of Congress are much more engaged in its “hidden half” than others. As an example, consider Representative Barbara Comstock (R-VA) and Senator Ted Cruz (R-TX). In 2016 alone, Comstock sent 1,508 letters to USCIS and 209 to the VA. Cruz, by contrast, sent only 449 letters to USCIS and 5 to the VA in that same year—despite representing over 28 million constituents in the state of Texas, compared with Comstock’s 770,000 constituents in Virginia’s 10th district. Comstock and Cruz anchor each end of the distribution of the amount of legislators’ correspondence with federal agencies. Across all agencies in 2016, Comstock sent 1,841 letters to the federal bureaucracy, while Cruz sent just 493. Together, they also illustrate the central question and puzzle of this book: why do legislators communicate with federal agencies, and why do some of them do so much more of this work than others?
In this book, we argue that these types of substantive representation beyond legislating belong under an overarching concept of interbranch representation.* We advance, measure, and explain a particular form of interbranch representation: how members of Congress work directly with federal agencies on behalf of various constituencies. Interbranch representation includes casework (constituency service) on behalf of individuals, nonprofits, and businesses, as well as oversight of executive branch policymaking and implementation. We show that interbranch representation is common but varies widely across members of Congress: as Comstock and Cruz illustrate, some provide a great deal to their constituents, while others provide almost none.
To explain why members of Congress engage in interbranch representation, we offer a unified framework that integrates and extends theories rooted in unequal demand, unequal legislator capacity, and varying strategic incentives to invest time and energy in interbranch representation as opposed to other activities like legislating, communications, or fundraising. Theoretically and empirically, the capacity of congressional offices is at the center of this framework. Unequal capacity consistently explains legislators’ interbranch work across a variety of domains. Constituent demand and legislators’ strategic incentives play important roles in shaping which constituents are served but have smaller effects on the amount of interbranch representation that a district receives. The strategic behavior we do see is associated with partisan/ideological and institutional context, not electoral incentives. Overall, our findings show how congressional offices can function akin to a bureaucratic “logic of appropriateness” when providing interbranch representation.
Interbranch representation has both broad and specific definitions. Broadly, it involves officials of one branch of government representing their constituents in the decision-making processes of another branch. In this book, we focus on interbranch representation that occurs between the legislative and executive branches of the United States government. Specifically, we examine requests that congressional offices send to federal agencies.2
Scholars have studied parts of interbranch representation under labels including “congressional oversight,” “constituency service” (Fenno 1978), “lettermarking” in the context of spending (Mills and Kalaf-Hughes 2015), “lobbying,” “backchannel representation,” “backdoor lawmaking,” or “policy representation” in the context of agency policymaking (Ritchie 2018, 2023; Ritchie and You 2019; Lauterbach and Ritchie 2025), “legislator advocacy” in the context of both constituent and donor service (Powell et al. 2023), “interbranch representation” in the context of legislators advising agency working groups (U.S. Department of Justice, Bureau of Justice Assistance 2016), and “interbranch representation of protected groups” in the context of descriptive representation in contacts to the bureaucracy (Lowande et al. 2019), or simply “representation” in the context of all types of requests to the bureaucracy (Judge-Lord et al. 2026). We adopt “interbranch representation” as an umbrella concept to describe all of these kinds of representational activities—any work on behalf of a constituency (or constituent), donor, business, industry, or district opinion on policy issues with another branch of government.
In recent years, scholars have begun to obtain snapshots of this work from federal agencies that are, unlike Congress, subject to the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) disclosure requirements. Acquiring these data is difficult, but doing so has yielded important findings on distributive politics (Mills and Kalaf-Hughes 2015), descriptive representation (Lowande et al. 2019), agency policymaking Ritchie (2023), legislative effectiveness (Kalaf-Hughes 2023), and money in politics (Powell et al. 2023). However, the lack of systematic data across all policy areas and agencies has necessarily limited the range of questions that could be explored with these data.
Our analysis in this book relies on the most comprehensive dataset of legislators’ interbranch activities to date. Through 434 Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests, we have obtained congressional correspondence logs from every department in the federal bureaucracy except the State Department.3 Together, these correspondence logs, which cover 2007 through 2024, capture over half a million instances of contact between members of Congress and federal agencies. Our work hand-coding these data allows us to identify on whose behalf legislators were advocating in each instance of contact.
We conceptualize interbranch representation as varying along two dimensions: the constituency represented (e.g., individuals, businesses, nonprofits, or local governments) and the type of representational activity undertaken (e.g., constituency service or policy work). This yields five sub-types of interbranch representation: (1) constituency service work on behalf of individual constituents, (2) constituency service work on behalf of businesses, (3) constituency service work on behalf of local governments or nonprofits, (4) general policy work with federal agencies, and (5) policy work with federal agencies on behalf of specific industries.4
To date, the activities that constitute these five sub-types of interbranch representation have been addressed by separate literatures. Constituency service has mostly been explored as reelection-oriented behavior (Cain et al. 1987), and until recently (e.g. Snyder 2024; Blackwood 2026), scholars have paid little attention to its role in representation. Scholarship on interactions between Congress and the executive branch has focused on strategic delegation of policymaking authority and appropriation of funds on the front end (Arnold 1979; Epstein and O’Halloran 1999; Kiewiet and McCubbins 1991) and oversight on the back end (McCubbins and Schwartz 1984).  Oversight scholarship focuses on hearings and investigations and rarely in terms of representation (but see Minta 2011). However, only a small share of congressional interactions with the executive branch rise to the level of hearings and investigations. The vast majority are interventions in the agency’s day-to-day operations (see, e.g., Lowande 2018; Lowande and Potter 2019). An interbranch representation perspective broadens the concept of oversight to encompass not only occasional hearings and oversight reports prompted by crises and scandals but also daily requests for information and comments on implementation. Overall, the concept of interbranch representation that we advance in this paper unifies constituency service, oversight, and other behaviors within a broader conceptual and empirical framework.
Interbranch representation includes advocacy on a wide range of subjects. Helping immigrants in their dealings with USCIS and veterans in their interactions with the VA are two very common forms of interbranch representation involving individual constituency service. Specifically, these actions might involve helping veterans check the status of their claims with the VA or helping immigrants file necessary forms. Other forms of individual constituency service might involve helping constituents obtain a tax refund with the IRS, helping constituents check their disability rating with the Social Security Administration, and helping Medicare beneficiaries navigate claims or access medical care.5
The most frequent requests that legislators make on behalf of businesses also involve immigration, as congressional offices help businesses obtain visas for their workers. Legislators also intervene in federal contracts, permits, rate cases, citations, fines, and loans, including loans for the Service-Disabled Veteran-Owned Small Business program. While Powell et al. (2023) found that members of Congress who receive more campaign donations from energy companies do more work helping energy companies secure permits and profitable rates, this is not the primary kind of corporate service we find. When we looked at who did the most work on behalf of businesses overall, we found progressive Democrat Senator Elizabeth Warren at the top of the list. This was puzzling at first, given past research and our own data showing that Republicans are more likely to represent business interests. Upon closer examination, however, we discovered what put Warren’s office on top: the extraordinary amount of work that her office did to help businesses get visas for workers with needed skills.
Interbranch representation on behalf of nonprofit organizations and local governments often involves legislators’ writing in support of grant applications or the many other ways that federal funds pass through state and local governments, police and fire departments, and nonprofits like Community Action Agencies.
Policy work, both generally and on behalf of industries, involves writing with comments on rules, requests for appearances at hearings, the implementation of legislation, and information about specific policy matters. Congressional offices also advocate for disaster declarations and aid and seek information about how appropriated money was spent and how regulatory and personnel decisions were made inside agencies.
In all of these instances of interbranch work, members of Congress are clearly engaging in some form of representation. Constituency service is perhaps most obviously a representational activity, as it involves legislators’ offices being responsive to constituents’ requests for help. Although some recent work has conceptualized constituency service as a key form of representation (Snyder 2024; Blackwood 2026), most work on constituency service has approached it as an activity that can help legislators electorally (e.g. Fiorina 1977; Cain et al. 1987). And while there is, of course, a vast literature on legislators’ representation of their constituents’ interests through legislative work, there is very little research exploring how legislators provide service to businesses or nonprofit organizations. Even when examining interbranch work as representation, prior studies have focused mostly on a single type of interbranch representation, showing that legislators engage in interbranch representation to represent constituents’ needs (Fiorina 1977; Fenno 1978; Mills and Kalaf-Hughes 2015; Powell et al. 2023; Snyder et al. 2025), constituents’ policy preferences (Ritchie 2018, 2023), shared identity groups (Lowande et al. 2019), or corporate donors (Powell et al. 2023).
By conceptualizing interbranch representation as including all five of these sub-types of constituency service and policy work, our book provides a new perspective on how members of Congress provide representation to their districts. Our data allow us to understand legislators’ service responsiveness, allocation responsiveness, and policy responsiveness (Eulau and Karps 1977) as provided through a single activity. Through these communications with federal agencies, members of Congress are providing service to their constituents, helping organizations within their districts obtain grants, and engaging in policy work. Our theory of Demand, Capacity, and Strategic Choices can help illuminate the extent to which legislators are acting as a “delegate” or “trustee” (Pitkin 1967) when providing interbranch representation. A significant role for constituent demand in shaping this work would suggest that legislators are following a delegate model and simply channeling their constituents’ demands to the federal bureaucracy. If, however, capacity and strategic choices also matter for interbranch representation, this picture of representation becomes more complicated. Indeed, we do find that the capacity of a legislator’s office ultimately governs their ability to meet this demand. Our book therefore reveals one way in which representation can depend on—and potentially be undermined by—the nature of a congressional office.
Our data capture the particular instance of contact between congressional offices and federal agencies that occurs as part of interbranch representation. As a whole, however, interbranch representation is an iterative process, and the components of this process inform the theory of this book. Because it involves both constituency service and policy work, much of interbranch representation may begin with a constituent becoming aware of some deficiency in the world and understanding it as a problem—particularly, a problem in which the federal government has a hand in either solving or creating. Second, the individual recognizes that congressional offices can help with this problem. Third, they contact a congressional office, which constitutes the demand part of our theory explaining interbranch representation. Fourth, the congressional office processes the request (per their capacity) and decides how to handle the request (in accordance with any strategy that they may wish to exercise). Finally, for the subset of cases for which such an action is appropriate and desired by the congressional office, the office will contact a federal agency. Our data capture these instances of contact.
Two other key features of interbranch representation are important to discuss further. First, as established above, legislators have a significant amount of discretion and autonomy in their decisions about engaging in interbranch representation, including where and how to direct these efforts. Party leaders constrain most other activities that legislators undertake, and even other activities where this constraint matters less, like position-taking, are highly public (e.g. Highton and Rocca 2005). Explaining why legislators engage in interbranch representation can therefore provide rich insight into legislative behavior that, given the importance of party and party leadership, previous work has largely been unable to reveal. Second, congressional staff are as important as legislators themselves for the activities that constitute interbranch representation. Staff are crucial for a number of functions in Congress (e.g. Hertel-Fernandez et al. 2019; Montgomery and Nyhan 2017; Crosson et al. 2020), particularly constituent-facing functions like constituency service (Grose et al. 2007; Landgrave and Weller 2020). Similarly, legislators themselves do not personally undertake all of the interbranch representation activities that they perform. Thus, our theory focuses as much on the capacity and other characteristics of the congressional office as it does on the decisions and characteristics of legislators.

title: 1  Interbranch Representation
text:
1.2 Why Study Interbranch Representation?
Our data make possible new inquiries into congressional behavior, representation, and legislative-executive interactions. We argue that a focus on legislative work in studies of these three areas has limited our understanding of them. By going beyond studying legislative behavior of members of Congress to examine how they engage with the federal bureaucracy to represent various constituencies, this book makes possible major new inquiries into the previously “hidden half of Congress.”
Scholarship on how members of the U.S. Congress represent their constituents has focused on legislative activity, including bill sponsorship (Schiller 1995; Rocca and Gordon 2010; Lazarus 2013; Waggoner 2019; Lauterbach et al. 2026; Yoel et al. 2026), roll-call votes (Rohde 1991; Poole and Rosenthal 1997; Ansolabehere et al. 2001; Ansolabehere and Jones 2010; Wallace 2014; Fowler 2026), committee participation (Hall 1987; Hall 1996; Gamble 2007; Ellis and Wilson 2013; Ban et al. 2022), and floor speeches (Maltzman and Sigelman 1996; Hill and Hurley 2002; Pearson and Dancey 2011b, 2011a; Kalaf-Hughes 2020). Importantly, all of these activities are highly visible to scholars, journalists, and constituents.

Much more, however, than votes and the text of bills that become law determines how government affects constituents. Federal agencies staffed by career civil servants and political appointees do a large share of policymaking as well as all policy implementation. Agencies make policy to meet the demands of changing technology and social relations, as well as the demands of changing presidential administrations, even when Congress is silent. And when Congress does manage to pass new laws, it inevitably instructs agencies to make and implement new policies. Even federal laws that empower state governments are almost always shaped and overseen by federal agencies. Given the prominent role of federal agencies in modern governance, it makes sense that members of Congress frequently involve themselves in executive branch policymaking and implementation to help their constituents, advocate for their districts, and advance their policy goals. However, the relative invisibility of this involvement has made it an under-studied part of representation. We have thus failed to assess our democracy on important grounds.

Empirical research that seeks to understand why members of Congress make the decisions that they do also focuses on legislative work. Models of legislative decision-making focus almost entirely on decisions about voting on bills (e.g., Kingdon 1977). In addition to being only half of what members of Congress actually do, legislative work is an inherently collective activity, in which legislators must build coalitions, gather information, and make decisions by working with other legislators. Such models are therefore inadequate for understanding how legislators engage in activities involving representation, including interbranch representation, which are much more decentralized. As a result of this focus on legislation, appropriations, and oversight hearings, scholars have characterized the modern Congress as centralized (Rohde 1991) and highly partisan (Lee 2009). But the constituency service and policy work we study here is neither. Unlike legislative activities that are often subject to constraints from party leaders, members of Congress have a great deal of autonomy over the amount and type of interbranch representation that they perform. Understanding why legislators engage in interbranch representation can provide valuable insight into legislators’ behavior absent these partisan and institutional constraints.


The focus on legislative work in both scholarship and popular media has additional implications for perceptions of Congress as an institution.  For years, Congress has been making headlines for appearing unproductive and dysfunctional, particularly according to legislative metrics like the passage of bills.6 Other collective failures, like the unprecedented Motion to Vacate that ended Kevin McCarthy’s Speakership in October of 2023 and the longest government shutdown in history that occurred in October and November of 2025, have highlighted Congress’s dysfunction to the public. Partisan polarization in Congress has been at an all-time high for over a decade, and although constituents largely approve of their individual legislators, these approval ratings are polarized by party.7


But running parallel to the gridlocked lawmaking activities is the work that legislative offices do to help constituents navigate the federal bureaucracy and shape executive branch policymaking. While many members of the public—and certainly the punditry—are aware of Congress’s legislative woes, fewer are aware of the other half of the work that congressional offices do behind the scenes to help constituents and shape executive-branch policymaking. Despite the fact that interbranch representation is largely hidden, only a tiny portion of these activities includes normatively suspect activities, like special work on behalf of corporate campaign donors. When we look closely at what congressional offices are doing, the vast majority of legislators’ requests, even those on behalf of business interests, are the kinds of things most people would want their representatives doing, suggesting that the institution of Congress is working to represent constituents and influence policy much more than one would think from reading the news.

   











Studying interbranch representation provides a more comprehensive picture of how Congress works and what it does. While focusing on legislative activities and legislators’ voting decisions is valuable, this view misses the 16,000 staffers who do most of the work. It also misses that half of that work involves working with or overseeing federal agencies.8 By refocusing attention on the bulk of the actual work done in legislators’ offices, we revisit core questions of political science: How should we understand the representative functions of members of Congress? Empirically, what do they do in office? How do we assess the quality of representation? How do the legislative and executive branches interact? Has it changed in recent years?



We find that, collectively, members of Congress make over a hundred thousand requests a year directly to executive branch officials. Unconstrained by legislative agendas and party discipline (Ritchie 2023), interbranch representation allows all members of Congress to directly shape the workings of government. However, we find that this work is highly variable — some members engage in extensive interbranch representation, and others do almost none.

These findings have implications for the study of representation in Congress, particularly how scholars conceive of the role of congressional staff and the extent to which representation is unconstrained by legislative agendas and party discipline. The role of congressional staff in interbranch work also speaks to how representation can be improved. More generally, because policy implementation is how the public interacts with government and experiences policy effects, the involvement of members of Congress at this stage of the process matters for representation.

title: 1  Interbranch Representation
text:
1.3 Variation in Interbranch Representation






When we first began collecting these data and having conversations with congressional scholars about interbranch representation, a common reaction we received was that every office provided constituency service, and that no significant variation in interbranch representation would exist.9 But a simple descriptive examination of our data quickly puts that notion to rest. Figure 4.3 below shows the average number of requests each legislator makes to federal agencies and reveals tremendous variation in interbranch representation in both the U.S. Senate (left) and the U.S. House of Representatives. In each figure, legislators are sorted by their percentile in the distribution in their chamber on the x-axis, from those with the lowest average levels of interbranch representation on the left to those with the highest on the right. As we will discuss in Section 3.1, the legislators at the top of this particular graph are the ones doing an unusually massive volume of work on behalf of immigrants seeking visas. Yet, when we remove immigration work, the pattern of inequality in constituency service persists. And, as we show in Section 3.5, when we remove constituency service casework, variation in policy work is no less extreme.
Figure 4.3 shows the tremendous variation in the amount of interbranch representation legislators provide to their constituents. This is the variation we aim to explain.



Figure 1.1: Observed levels of interbranch representation per legislator per year







(a) Senate











(b) House













One of the more striking features here is that on average over this period, the House and the Senate display similar within-chamber variation in interbranch representation. This is despite the fact that in the House all members represent similar numbers of constituents, while in the Senate constituent populations vary substantially.
The group of high performers includes a somewhat surprising mix. While both Kirsten Gillibrand and Chuck Schumer, who represent the relatively populous state of New York, are among those who do large amounts of interbranch representation, so is Robert Byrd, representing the much smaller state of West Virginia. Other New York legislators, including Grace Meng and Dan Donovan, are also high performers, and there is other geographic overlap among the most prolific providers of interbranch representation: House members and senators from Florida and Virginia are part of this group. Two of them, Frank Wolf and Barbara Comstock, even consecutively represented the same district. These patterns suggest that some idiosyncratic form of demand—perhaps something specific to these states or their constituents—could be driving interbranch representation. However, the patterns evident in this figure raise other possibilities. Most notably, Comstock worked as the chief of staff for Frank Wolf, which suggests that something about the way their offices operate could be contributing to their high levels of work on interbranch representation. Because senators’ staff sizes vary according to state population, Byrd’s office would not have had the same staff capacity as Gillibrand’s or Schumer’s. Furthermore, all of these top performers have faced very different electoral environments: while Comstock narrowly lost reelection in 2018, Meng has frequently won reelection without facing a Republican opponent. We therefore look beyond simple demand-related factors to explain interbranch representation.

title: 1  Interbranch Representation
section: 1.4 Our Theoretical Framework and Key Concepts
text:
1.4 Our Theoretical Framework and Key Concepts



We gather disparate scholarship into a unified framework of Demand, Capacity, and Strategic Choices to explain variation in interbranch representation, integrating and extending theories rooted in unequal demand, unequal legislator (and legislative office) capacity, and varying strategic motivations to invest time and energy in interbranch representation as opposed to other activities like legislating, communications, or fundraising. Prior work has typically studied these activities — and their explanations — piecemeal, focusing on one type of activity and a narrower set of causes at a time. To explain variation in different types of interbranch representation, studies have focused on institutional position (Lowande 2018; Lowande and Potter 2019; Lauterbach and Ritchie 2025; Judge-Lord et al. 2026), experience (Ritchie 2018, 2023; Lowande 2018; Judge-Lord et al. 2026), or party status and partisan alignment (Ritchie 2018, 2023; Powell et al. 2023; Lowande 2018, 2019; Lauterbach and Ritchie 2025). Theories also suggest that interbranch representation ought to be driven by ideological alignment and electoral competition (Fiorina 1977; Rivers and Fiorina 1989; King 1991), but these intuitions are largely unsupported by empirical work (Lowande 2018; Ritchie 2018, 2023). Our aim in this book is to integrate types of behavior and explanations to provide a more comprehensive assessment of the drivers of interbranch representation.


Demand. We define Demand as the constituent-driven influences on a congressional office. In any democratic system, the needs and preferences of a legislator’s constituents are supposed to play a role in the work done by a legislator’s office. While a large literature exists examining whether and how constituents’ policy preferences impact legislators’ voting behavior (Miller and Stokes 1963; Achen and Bartels 2016), less is known about how constituent demand relates to the provision of interbranch representation.
Capacity. We define Capacity as the ability of a legislator’s office to produce work. We argue that the amount of interbranch representation that legislators engage in is likely to be positively associated with the capacity of the legislator’s office. Member offices with greater capacity have the potential to provide more interbranch representation, while the inverse is true for offices with less capacity. We are building on four branches of capacity literature: (1) formal theory voter screening models that predict that as a legislator’s capacity increases, they will increase their level of constituency service (Ashworth and Bueno de Mesquita 2006), (2) empirical research that suggests low congressional capacity serves as a major constraint on Congress’s work (LaPira et al. 2020; Reynolds 2020; Bolton and Thrower 2016, 2022), (3) empirical research that shows legislator capacity impacts backchannel (backdoor) policymaking — when legislators contact executive agencies attempting to influence policy (Ritchie 2018, 2023), and (4) our prior research that shows that increases in congressional capacity can offset shifts in legislator priorities between policymaking and constituency service (Judge-Lord et al. 2026).
Strategic Responses to the Political Environment. We define Strategic Choices as decisions legislators make about what to prioritize and how to allocate their time and resources in response to the political environment (partisan, electoral, and institutional conditions a member faces in a given year). How much energy and staff time do legislators want to devote to interbranch representational activities as opposed to other tasks like legislating, communicating, and fundraising? Similarly, how much time and energy do they want to devote to different types of interbranch representational activities? We argue that the answer depends on what legislators are trying to accomplish and the political environment that shapes their ability to achieve their goals. Beginning with Fenno (1973) and Mayhew (1974), a substantial body of legislative politics literature has explored the strategic motivations of members of Congress.
In this book, we examine a variety of strategic choices, drawing on established literatures on reelection motivation (Fenno 1973; Mayhew 1974; Fiorina 1977; Cain et al. 1987; Serra and Cover 1992; Serra and Moon 1994; Dropp and Peskowitz 2012), ideological motivations (Lowande 2019), obstacles in the legislative process (such as being in the minority party) changing incentives to engage in backdoor policymaking (Ritchie 2023), committee assignments that position members to engage in policy oversight of specific agencies (Lowande 2019; Lowande and Potter 2019), and being a member of the president’s party shaping anticipated cooperation from the executive branch (Berry et al. 2010).
Notably, several of these strategic motivations provide different expectations for different types of interbranch representation. For example, the substantial body of reelection incentives literature suggests re-election-focused legislators would want to engage in constituency service (e.g., King 1991; Ashworth and Bueno de Mesquita 2006). On the other hand, Ritchie’s findings in Backdoor Lawmaking showed no consistent relationship between electoral vulnerability and policy work with federal agencies (Ritchie 2023). In this book, we provide both a general theory of interbranch representation and distinct hypotheses for each of our subtypes of interbranch representation.

title: 1  Interbranch Representation
text:
1.5 Why Interbranch Representation Matters

Impact of Federal Bureaucracy on the Lives of Americans
In addition to the policy impacts of bureaucratic regulations, which range from vehicle and product safety to the use of REAL IDs, the federal bureaucracy affects the lives of many Americans more directly. Federal agencies administer programs and distribute benefits to millions of Americans. Over 75 million Americans received Social Security benefits in April of 2026. In Fiscal Year 2023, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) processed over 10 million requests and naturalized nearly 900,000 new U.S. citizens. Between 1970 and 2025, the Department of Labor paid over $18 billion in benefits to coal miners suffering from black lung. By keeping seniors out of poverty, by granting citizenship and its rights to immigrants, by compensating coal miners for their illness and suffering, and by administering many similar programs, the federal bureaucracy directly touches individuals’ lives in profound ways. The federal government employs over two million civil servants who use their expertise to administer these programs and serve the American public. Recent reductions in the federal workforce by the Trump administration have laid bare the impacts of the federal bureaucracy on regional employment, in addition to policy implementation and the delivery of services. And as recent government shutdowns have made clear, many Americans depend on the federal government for a paycheck, in addition to the public’s dependence on the federal government for basic safety and regulatory measures.
As former member of Congress and political scientist David E. Price described, “Congressional casework often provides a kind of appeals process for bureaucratic decisions, a function that has sometimes been likened to that of the ombudsman in Scandinavian countries. It is not an ideal mechanism… It would be preferable to have all comers receive fair and efficient service from the agencies in the first place” (Price 2022, pg 101). In an ideal world, as Congressman Price argued, the federal bureaucracy would administer its programs with no errors or delays. Beneficiaries would receive timely responses to their queries, and agencies would have the capacity to handle unexpected surges in demand for assistance. In practice, however, this is not the case. Bureaucratic processes will always be vulnerable to human error, and in such instances, constituents will need help addressing these errors. Although some programs are designed with “administrative burdens” to make them less appealing for the public to use (Herd and Moynihan 2019), even minimally burdensome agencies, like the Social Security Administration, can make mistakes that require intervention. Members of Congress, as elected representatives, are well positioned to help their constituents with these problems. And there need not be a bureaucratic error or failure for a constituent to reach out for help: the standard language for casework requests on legislators’ official websites makes it clear that constituents can ask for help “if [they] feel [they] have been treated unfairly” in an interaction with a federal agency. Constituency service, then, can say as much about constituents’ perceptions of fairness as it can about the functioning of the federal bureaucracy.
For these and many other reasons, constituent demand for interbranch representation is difficult to measure precisely. But differences in interbranch representation can tell us much about how members of Congress choose to serve their constituents and why some constituents receive more of this help than others. As we discuss in the next section, interbranch representation can also help to inform our understanding of the relationship between the legislative and executive branches.



Reshaping Our Understanding of How Legislative and Executive Branches Interact
In studying interactions between Congress and the executive branch, political scientists have focused on formal delegation, bargaining over legislation, and oversight hearings. While important, modern scholarship neglects the bulk of how legislators actually interact with the executive branch, which is much less based on formal legal authority and constitutionally prescribed roles that ground most models of interbranch relations. While certainly operating in the shadow of formal oversight, lawmaking, and budgeting powers, interbranch representation mostly relies on norms and softer forms of legitimacy. From an interbranch representation perspective, “separation of powers” is a misleading moniker. The behavior we document involves formal and informal mechanisms by which legislators influence how the executive branch makes and implements policy, but there is little separation.
Being in the “legislative branch” often prevents us from seeing congressional offices as bureaucracies with functions in the broader system of the U.S. government. Including, but far beyond, “fire alarm” oversight, legislators are involved at every level and stage of bureaucratic politics. There is constant communication between legislators and agencies, including requests tagged as “VIP” that expedite bureaucratic procedures and elevate decisions to higher layers of the federal agency in question. Members of Congress function as a complaint and appeals process for the allocation of benefits, grants, permits, and contracts. They function as powerful allies to advocacy and lobbying campaigns. In short, we should think about congressional offices as part of the network of institutions that make government tick. The functioning of one interacts with the functioning of the other in a broader system of government.

While members of Congress are often intervening on behalf of their constituents when they encounter problems with the federal government, we can also think of these interactions more neutrally, as simply one institution filling gaps left by the other. The ability of legislators to connect constituents to a vast and sprawling bureaucracy is valuable both in good times and in bad. Constant, rapid changes in the world lead to changes in how constituents experience the federal government, which necessarily involves some amount of friction with the federal bureaucracy. To fully fulfill its representational duties, Congress should have the capacity to reduce that friction.
Numerous examples from our data illustrate how interbranch representation, especially individual constituency service, is not always undertaken because constituents are experiencing a problem that originated in the federal bureaucracy, even though it does involve the federal bureaucracy. For instance, Representative Bob Gibbs wrote to the Office of Congressional and Intergovernmental Affairs within the Department of Labor on November 26, 2019, on behalf of a constituent who was having trouble creating an online account as part of the process of permanently hiring a foreign worker. Although some government websites, like HealthCare.gov, have famously experienced widespread problems, other, more idiosyncratic problems are common features of nearly all websites. The difficulty could also have been the result of simple user error. In this case, it is valuable that Gibbs was able to reach out to the relevant agency on the constituent’s behalf and provide the kind of representation that would allow them to take this action for their business.
A similar example comes from a letter that Senator Cory Gardner sent to the National Park Service (NPS) within the Department of the Interior on June 9, 2017. Gardner was writing on behalf of a “constituent requesting insurance information from a driver that caused his accident.” Presumably, the driver was an employee of the NPS, but aside from that fact, nothing about the constituent’s need in this specific incident was unique to a government agency. Requesting insurance information from other drivers is a routine part of handling the aftermath of a car accident. It does not indicate that a bureaucratic process within the NPS is fundamentally broken. In fact, depending on how many similar situations the NPS has experienced, it is possible that they could institute or revise procedures within the agency for dealing with such cases that arise because of unexpected events.
More generally, our dataset contains a large number of letters, mostly sent to the Department of Veterans’ Affairs (VA) and various Department of Labor subagencies, in which constituents are simply requesting the status of the claims that they have filed with these agencies. While these contacts could be the result of a lack of communication from the agency and/or a particularly slow processing speed when it comes to handling claims and requests, they do not appear to be driven entirely by things in the bureaucracy that are fundamentally broken.
Rather than indicating a fully broken system of government, these interactions between the legislative and executive branches suggest that, holistically, the system can work, especially when it comes to representing constituents. Indeed, studies of congressional oversight of the bureaucracy or the legislative process that ignore the role of interbranch representation are missing potentially important parts of the picture. As Kenneth G. Olson so eloquently describes,

“…responding to constituents’ complaints and problems provides a recurring opportunity for a member to scrutinize the work of the executive and judicial branches….Characteristically, this scrutiny takes the form of interfering in federal administrative processes on specific issues of complaint. Sometimes such interference goes beyond the individual issue concerned and results in systematic changes in administrative procedures. Occasionally it leads to corrective legislation. In any event, the mere threat of congressional intervention helps ensure that the federal bureaucracy will anticipate problems before they arise and will not neglect its duties. Thus the exercise of the service function infuses new life into the theory of Congress as a check on the other branches of government and as a kind of balance-wheel within the entire system of government.”
—– (Olson 1966, pgs 338-339)

title: 1  Interbranch Representation
section: 1.6 The “Hidden Half” of the Broken Branch?
text:
1.6 The “Hidden Half” of the Broken Branch?
Members of Congress make choices about how much effort to allocate to interbranch representation in terms of both staff and time, as well as which topics and policies to work on and whom to represent. These choices are constrained by their capacity and sometimes driven by events of the day. But unlike other aspects of the job, these choices are not constrained by public attention from either constituents or the media. Rather, these choices are made behind the scenes, and the consequences of those decisions are largely invisible to constituents and journalists. Members of Congress are not required to disclose or report how much constituency service or interbranch representation they have provided. Indeed, as we discovered firsthand, it is exceedingly difficult and time-consuming for academics to track down that information.
Given the budget constraints and challenges facing journalists today, it is almost unthinkable that a journalist could track down the necessary records to show that Senator X or Congressman Y is one of the worst-performing Members of Congress in this regard. Savvy legislators thinking rationally about how to allocate their scarce time and resources may choose to allocate their attention elsewhere to areas that may be more public-facing—such as communications staff or legislative work like introducing bills. They may hesitate to short-staff work that receives media attention, especially votes on bills, which have received more attention of late as a closely divided Congress makes every vote important (Desjardins et al. 2026).
We argue that interbranch representation is unique because it is invisible—it is work in which legislators engage when the public at large is not looking. This “hidden half of Congress” is difficult for academics to measure, difficult for journalists to cover, and, perhaps most importantly, difficult for voters to monitor. Almost by definition, this is a topic that we know very little about. In contrast to visible forms of representation like roll call voting, bill sponsorship, congressional press releases, and social media posts that have received considerable scholarly attention, invisible forms of representation like constituent service and advocating to the bureaucracy about policy issues have received much less attention.

Much has been written about Congress as the “Broken Branch” of American government (Mann and Ornstein 2006; LaPira et al. 2020). While explanations for why this is the case have varied, scholars have consistently shown the drop in Congress’s capacity to legislate (Binder 2015). This literature has largely focused on Congress’s most visible legislative work — sponsoring bills and casting roll call votes — which has received extensive scholarly scrutiny. Some limited attention has been paid to the public actions of congressional committees, such as roll call votes within committees, committee assignment requests, committee assignments, committee transfers, and passing bills out of committees. Measures of legislative effectiveness are built on these visible actions of representation (Volden and Wiseman 2014).
Amid the dysfunction that has been apparent in recent Congresses, some observers have noted that the institution nevertheless is capable of passing some legislation, often with bipartisan support. Dubbed the “Secret Congress,” this part of the institution receives far less media attention yet appears much more functional and cooperative, thus obscuring the positive legislative work of Congress from public view. Critics of this theory, however, argue that this obfuscation of bipartisan cooperation is detrimental to democracy. From this perspective, constituents’ ignorance of this facet of Congress defeats its purpose.
The “hidden half of Congress” that we examine in this book goes far beyond the “Secret Congress” that works well to pass bipartisan legislation. Instead of a more functional version of the legislation-focused Congress with which the public is already familiar, interbranch representation is an altogether different type of work, and many constituents are unaware that Congress is undertaking this work at all. This ignorance of interbranch representation exists despite the fact that it helps to represent constituents and forms a large component of the workload shouldered by congressional offices. By that logic, its obfuscation is even more detrimental to democracy. In what follows, we provide the first evidence systematically documenting interbranch representation and its extraordinary variation.

title: 1  Interbranch Representation
text:
1.7 Organization of the Book
In Chapter 2, we review the existing literature on interbranch representation and introduce our unifying framework of Demand, Capacity, and Motivation to conceptually organize explanations for variation in overall levels of interbranch representation as well as each of our five sub-types of interbranch representation. Existing work that focuses on narrower explanations and typically just one of these outcomes misses variation in who is being represented—individual constituents, businesses, or nonprofits—and the relationship between policy work and constituency service work. These activities are linked, not only because they come from a common budget of effort and time, but also because one often leads to the other. Casework and oversight are more connected than scholarship that studies them separately implies.10 Moreover, many activities that fit in our framework (e.g., advocacy on behalf of local governments) are missed by the existing triad of legislation, oversight, and casework representing individual constituents. We explain how our theory builds on existing theories of representation.
In Chapter 3, we introduce and describe our five types of interbranch representation: constituency service on behalf of individuals, businesses, and nonprofits and local governments, as well as general policy work and policy work on behalf of specific industries. We provide a rich qualitative overview of what each of these types looks like in our data. Individual constituency service covers “classic” cases such as requests for help obtaining veterans’ benefits and help with immigration paperwork—but it also includes a number of surprising requests that might not obviously be connected to a federal agency. Corporate service involves helping businesses obtain things like permits, grants, and visas for foreign workers, while also responding to esoteric concerns that business owners (mostly of small businesses) bring to the attention of their legislators. Service on behalf of nonprofit organizations and local governments focuses on supporting applications that these organizations have submitted for competitive grants. Both general policy work and policy work on behalf of industries involve legislators intervening before legislation is passed and during the implementation of legislation, often by writing about proposed rules. We make two major points about our data here that inform the interpretation of our analyses. First, constituency service has the potential to inform policy work by bringing widespread issues to legislators’ attention. Second, legislators’ success in intervening in agencies’ policy work depends on how willing the agencies are to respond.
Chapter 4 describes the processes by which we collected, coded, and processed our data, before providing a quantitative overview of the content of and variation in our five types of interbranch representation. We obtained our data through a large number of Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests over a 10-year period, which has produced a near-census of congressional contacts with federal agencies. The vast majority of these communications involve individual constituency service. Although much of this work is routine, major events like natural disasters, economic crises, and the COVID-19 pandemic also appear to influence the content of this type of interbranch representation. Across legislators, we document extraordinary variation in all five types of interbranch representation: some do very large amounts, while others do almost none. And although many legislators who are high performers of one type are also high performers of other types, this is not always the case. These descriptive findings help to further motivate one of the central questions of this book: Why do some members of Congress do so much more interbranch representation than others?
Chapter 5 we consider how constituent demand shapes interbranch representation. Because Congress does not make constituent requests public, we cannot observe demand directly. Instead, we test whether interbranch representation varies with three possible sources of variation in constituent demand that we can measure with Census data: how many constituents a legislator represents, how many are empowered to seek help, and how many need help from the federal government. We find that each of these sources of demand shapes interbranch representation, but the type of work depends on where the demand comes from. The number of constituents shapes constituency service more than policy work, though senators from larger states do far more of every type of interbranch work. One complication here is that state population is bundled with larger office budgets in the Senate, which may increase their capacity—a topic we focus on in the following chapter. Empowered constituents generate different kinds of work: legislators with more government workers do more constituency service, while those with more college graduates do more policy work. Finally, legislators representing households with greater need do more work on behalf of nonprofits and local governments, but not more constituency service for individuals. For greater-needs individual constituents, the disempowerment associated with greater needs outweighs the need-based reasons to reach out, such that the needs of low-income constituents reach Congress largely through organizations rather than individual requests.
In Chapter 6 we examine how the capacity of congressional offices shapes interbranch representation. Legislators can respond to constituent demand, and generate work of their own, only to the extent their offices have the ability to do so. We test four sources of capacity: legislator experience, staff, committee leadership positions, and seats on an agency’s reporting committee. Because many of these change over a legislator’s career, we compare legislators with one another and also compare the same legislator before and after their capacity changes. We find that capacity matters: capacity that comes from experience in Congress and larger staff increases many types of interbranch representation. In contrast, capacity that comes from committee roles (leadership positions or a seat on an agency’s reporting committee) increases general policy work.
In Chapter 7 we examine how the political environment shapes the strategic incentives for legislators to engage in interbranch representation. How do incentives shape who is represented and the kinds of work congressional offices prioritize? In this chapter, we explore how incentives shape decisions about how much to prioritize interbranch representation, what type of interbranch activity to do (policy or constituency service), and on whose behalf to do it (constituents, companies, nonprofits, or local governments). We find that interbranch representation is shaped by partisan, ideological, electoral, and institutional incentives. Generally, we find alignment (working with allies) outweighs antagonism in driving interbranch work. On the electoral side, we see House members in competitive districts doing more constituency service, but no evidence that this is causal. However, competitive primaries may cause House members to increase constituency service. Institutionally, we see majority status inducing members of the House to do more policy work and less constituency service work, but no change in Senators’ behavior. Finally, supporting staff allocation as a plausible mechanism by which priorities translate to differences in representation, we find that allocating more staff to a given type of interbranch work leads to more of that work getting done.
We conclude in Chapter 8 with a discussion of what our results mean for how we should think about the institution of Congress and the role of legislator offices in a democracy. This includes several analyses of how interbranch representation aligns with other ways of assessing the volume or style of representation, such as Legislative Effectiveness and Legislative Styles. Finally, we look prospectively at the future of interbranch representation, explore the policy implications of our findings for how interbranch representation can be improved, and discuss how interbranch representation may be changing during the Trump administration.
